title: Who was working at the same time?
subtitle: Use Artline's timelines to turn a date into a question.
introduction: An artist's name often arrives with a period attached: Renaissance, Impressionism, modern art. Those labels are useful, but they can make the past look tidier than it was. A timeline lets you start somewhere else—with people whose lives overlapped, works made a few years apart, or a book published while a painter was still at work.
Begin with the [artist timeline](https://artlines.org/). Choose a stretch of years you can take in at a glance. You can widen it later.

sections.title: Put two lives side by side
paragraphs: Find an artist you know, then look at someone whose dates overlap. Were they at similar stages of their lives? Did one career begin as the other ended? Open their records and compare a few works. Sharing a lifetime is a useful place to start, but the works will tell you more than two bars on a chart.

The initial view is a popular selection. Turn off **Only popular painters** when you want to go beyond those names. Country and regional filters refer to artists' recorded associations; a museum's location is a different question.

sections.title: Read the date twice
paragraphs: First notice where a work sits on the timeline. Then read its date label. “About 1650” and “1640–1660” carry different information, even if a chart places both near the same point. Keep that uncertainty when taking notes or quoting a record.
An empty stretch in an artist's catalogue may tell you about the available records, rather than the artist's productivity. For an undated work, the year remains an open question.

sections.title: Bring in a book or an event
paragraphs: Switch to the [combined timeline](https://artlines.org/all) to put artworks beside literature and historical events. Or give one subject more room with the [books](https://artlines.org/books) and [events](https://artlines.org/events) views.

Try a narrow question: what else falls within the decade around a painting? Follow a record that surprises you. If you want to argue that a particular book influenced an artist, look for evidence that connects them—a letter, a documented encounter, a source cited in the record. Proximity on a timeline supplies the question, not the answer.

sections.title: Follow a work to its collection
paragraphs: The [museum directory](https://artlines.org/museums) offers a different route. Start with a collection, choose a work, then return to its artist and date. This is especially useful when preparing for a visit: two pictures in the same building may belong to very different historical settings.
Artline's collection totals count the records included here. For the museum's holdings, current displays and visiting arrangements, follow its official information.

sections.title: Keep the source with the note
paragraphs: When a detail becomes useful to your research, save its source link along with the title, date and artist. The linked collection record may explain an attribution, record a change of date or provide a bibliography. If you plan to reuse an image, read its permissions separately.
You do not need to cover a whole century in one sitting. Two works, a date you had not noticed and a source worth following can be enough for a productive visit to the timeline.
